messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 50

At sixty-seven, he still carries himself like a man who has spent decades walking into courtrooms. Shoulders squared. Suit pressed. Gray hair combed back. But lately, the weight of the morning feels heavier. He sits at his desk before the first hearing, staring at a case file he has read three times. The words blur. His mind drifts to a place he does not want to go.

It happened thirty-two years ago, when he was a junior prosecutor in a district attorney’s office. His supervising attorney—a man he respected, a mentor—called him into a private office after hours to review a plea deal. There was no review. There was a hand on his shoulder, then a grip on his tie, then a voice that switched from praise to threat. He remembers the stale coffee on the man’s breath, the weight of his body against the desk, the sharp pain, the long silence afterward. He never reported it. He told himself it was a show of power, nothing more. He transferred to a different unit. He never spoke of it. Not to his wife, not to anyone.

For years, he pushed the memory down. He threw himself into work—long hours, complex cases, convictions that made the evening news. He married, had children, built a life that looked solid from the outside. His wife knew he had a temper, that he sometimes woke up thrashing in the dark, that he kept a loaded revolver in his nightstand. She attributed it to the stress of his career. He let her.

Then she died. Three years ago. Cancer. And the structure he had built to keep the memory locked inside began to crack.

Now he lives alone in the same house. He does not sleep more than four hours a night. When he closes his eyes, he sees the cheap wood-grain desk, hears the lock click, feels the pressure against his wrists. Sometimes he wakes up on the floor, heart pounding, sheets twisted. He has stopped going to the office cafeteria. The smell of burnt coffee and the sound of laughter from a corner table pull him back to that room. He eats lunch at his desk with the door locked.

At work, his colleagues notice changes. He used to relish cross-examinations. Now he avoids eye contact with male witnesses. He has asked the court coordinator to assign him to a different courtroom—the one on the second floor, with the windows and the natural light, because the fluorescent hum of the other courtroom makes his hands shake. He tells himself it is a preference. He knows it is a trap.

He has stopped visiting his wife’s grave. The cemetery is too quiet, too open. He feels watched. He carries a pocketknife now, something he never did before. When someone walks too close behind him in a hallway, his jaw locks. He replays the assault in his mind during depositions, sometimes missing entire questions. He has shouted at a paralegal for entering his office without knocking. He apologized, but the apology felt hollow.

He thinks about the assault every day. He does not call it that. He calls it “that night.” He tells himself it was not rape because he did not fight back, because he went into the office willingly, because he was young and scared and the man was powerful. He has read about statutes of limitations. He knows the window is closed. But sometimes, in the middle of a closing argument, he imagines standing up in a different courtroom and saying what happened. The fantasy lasts only a moment. Then the shame fills his chest like smoke.

He has not touched another person since his wife died. Not a handshake, not a hug. He avoids the subway. He drives to work, even in gridlock, so he does not have to stand pressed against strangers. Last week, a security guard at the courthouse put a hand on his arm to stop him, and he flinched so violently that the guard asked if he was okay. He said he was fine. He is not fine.

The case file on his desk waits. He picks up his pen. His hand trembles. He puts the pen down.
